transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Rajiv Patel (Pandora CTO), Sofia Martinez (Pandora Platform Eng), Evan Brooks (Pandora SecOps)

Auto-generated Summary: discussed dedicated vs private deployment options, isolation needs, burst/failover strategy, and next steps for pilot.

[00:00:05] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining on valentines, uh, afternoon. quick round‑robin? you can, you know, say name and role

[00:00:14] Rajiv (CTO): Rajiv, CTO at Pandora Systems, hi, thanks for setting this up

[00:00:18] Sofia (Plat Eng): Sofia, platform, I own infra for inference services

[00:00:21] Evan (SecOps): Evan, secops, i'll be focused on encryption and logs, thanks

[00:00:25] Maya: awesome. Liam, do you want to frame the agenda?

[00:00:29] Liam (Redwood SE): yeah, thanks. high level: we want to understand your QPS/latency targets, model sizes, how bursty the traffic is, and any isolation or on‑prem requirements. then we can map to reserved GPU counts, warm pool / burst design, and security touch points. also we'll propose a pilot plan for benchmarking. sound good?

[00:00:47] Rajiv: yeah that's perfect. to give context, we run a mix of small LLMs for product search and a few larger instruction models for summary and code assist. peak tokens/sec is kind of spikey, like during release windows and daytime dashboards. we currently use an in‑house k8s cluster and some EC2 gpus for batched jobs.

[00:01:12] Sofia: to add, our 99th p latency requirement for real‑time features is ~200ms for short prompts (<=512 tokens). for longer completion or batch jobs we accept higher latencies but throughput matters for cost.

[00:01:28] Liam: got it. are the real‑time calls latency sensitive end‑to‑end or is some client‑side async acceptable?

[00:01:34] Rajiv: end‑to‑end; customers expect near realtime. if you hit over 300ms they notice.

[00:01:39] Maya: ok that gives us a target. can you share rough traffic shape—baseline rps and spikes or percentiles?

[00:01:46] Sofia: baseline is about 40 RPS for the small models, peaks up to 120 RPS for short prompts; for the large models baseline is 2–3 RPS and peaks to 12 during heavy times. tokens per request vary. we'll share traces.

[00:02:05] Liam: great, that helps. first question on tenancy: do you need physical isolation (single‑tenant GPUs) or is logical isolation plus quota and warm pool acceptable?

[00:02:15] Rajiv: security team prefers dedicated tenancy for the large model workloads—esp the code assist stuff that touches infra keys—so for those we'd like dedicated nodes if possible. for the smaller models we can tolerate multi‑tenant warm pools.

[00:02:28] Evan: yeah, and we need to ensure no cross‑tenant KV leak, i.e., KV cache isolation. also we have strict KMS controls, HSM for signing, and we audit all access.

[00:02:36] Liam: okay that's a common pattern: hybrid mix—reserved dedicated capacity for sensitive models, shared warm pools for scale. Redwood Dedicated supports GPU pools where you can pin model versions to a pool and apply tenant fencing. we also have private deployments (VPC or on‑prem) if you need the control plane to be inside your network.

[00:02:55] Rajiv: curious on the difference between dedicated and private in practical terms—does private change the way burst works?

[00:03:02] Liam: good question. private means your control plane is customer‑managed (or on‑prem) and inference nodes can be in your VPC or datacenter. you still can have reserved capacity and warm pools but burst across Redwood's hosted capacity isn't available when fully on‑prem—unless you route through a hybrid. so tradeoff: maximum isolation vs ability to burst to Redwood hosted when you suddenly spike.

[00:03:26] Maya: to that point, a hybrid approach is possible: keep critical models on private/dedicated nodes and allow non‑critical traffic to overflow to hosted pools with encryption in transit and contractual SLOs.

[00:03:37] Evan: overflow is interesting, we need to see encryption keys and e2e KMS integration. our compliance folks will ask where keys are stored. does Redwood support external KMS/HSM?

[00:03:46] Liam: yes, we integrate with customer KMS solutions — we can do centralized key wrapping and HSM integration. we'll share the KMS integration doc. there are some caveats when you want to do on‑prem HSM + hosted burst; keys must be available to nodes doing inference or use envelope encryption patterns.

[00:04:04] Rajiv: also want to discuss cost — what's the pricing model for reserved nodes vs on‑demand burst? we need rough numbers for exec.

[00:04:12] Maya: we'll put together a TCO spreadsheet after we get the model sizes and traffic traces. ballpark, reserved capacity is monthly committed with a unit price for the GPU type, and burst/overage is billed at on‑demand rates. we'll send a sample calc.

[00:04:24] Sofia: for sizing - our largest model is a 70B parameter model quantized to 4‑bit for inference, and smaller ones are 7B and 3B. the 70B is what we want isolated. any recommendations for GPU type?

[00:04:36] Liam: for a 70B, recommended is multi‑GPU A100/RTX8000 class or next‑gen L4/RTX depending on sequence lengths and KV cache patterns. with quantization profiles we often run these on 8x A100 or 4–8x L4 depending on perf. we'll need to profile with your token lengths; recommend a small benchmark run to pick the right footprint.

[00:04:58] Rajiv: we have token lengths that vary a lot — code assist uses fairly short context (1k), summaries go up to 4k. does that change the GPU selection?

[00:05:07] Liam: yes longer context increases KV cache and memory needs; also runtime kernels differ. sometimes a slightly larger GPU with more memory gives better latency than aggressive sharding. we'll profile both.

[00:05:18] Maya: operational question: how do we handle prewarming? some of our spikes are only 5–15 minutes and if we cold start, we blow latency SLOs.

[00:05:25] Liam: warm pools and pre‑warmed hot nodes are our typical mitigation. Redwood Dedicated offers both guaranteed reserved nodes that are always warm and a warm pool that can scale with prewarm heuristics. you can set burst guardrails — e.g., max scale per minute and a failover model variant for latency vs cost tradeoff.

[00:05:43] Sofia: what's the prewarm time? if we need a hot node in under 30 seconds is that feasible?

[00:05:49] Liam: depends on model size; for a 70B cold start with sharding can be minutes. prewarmed nodes keep KV cache primed; warm pool warmup usually takes 20–90s depending on kernel/loading strategy. for strict sub‑30s we recommend reserved hot nodes or a smaller model fallback.

[00:06:06] Rajiv: fallback models — how transparent is routing? can we A/B or automatically fall to quantized variants?

[00:06:11] Liam: yes, routing policies support automatic fallback. you can define latency SLOs and cost/window policies so requests automatically route to a compatible variant or a cached prefix model. we can also do canary rollouts.

[00:06:23] Evan: audit logs — we need per‑token request logs for compliance and RL review. retention is a must. what are your existing capabilities?

[00:06:29] Maya: Redwood Console provides token‑level breakdowns and per‑route traces. retention can be customized as an add‑on; we can pull logs into your SIEM via log forwarders and we support structured traces. we'll include the logging SLA in the security doc.

[00:06:43] Sofia: network wise, we want everything over private peering and no public egress for certain models. can you do VPC peering for dedicated clusters?

[00:06:50] Liam: yes VPC peering and private link patterns are supported for Dedicated and Private. for hosted burst you'd need a controlled egress pattern and contractual guarantees; we can work with network team to define allowed egress endpoints.

[00:07:03] Rajiv: curious about failure modes — if a reserved pool is full because of tenant isolation, can we failover to other regions or is that blocked by isolation policy?

[00:07:12] Liam: isolation can be defined at pool level. if it's strict single‑tenant and on‑prem, failover is limited. for dedicated but hosted, you can define fallback to a compatible model variant in another region or allow limited spillover with contractual protections. we usually implement prioritized routing: primary pool -> secondary pool -> model variant fallback -> queued requests.

[00:07:35] Maya: with customers that have strict isolation we often propose a 'hybrid guardrail'—keep critical models in dedicated private nodes with autoscaling but allow explicit, auditable overflow to a Redwood-hosted pool under certain contract conditions.

[00:07:47] Rajiv: ok that helps. let's talk pilot scope: what does Redwood usually run for a two‑week pilot to validate performance?

[00:07:55] Liam: typical pilot includes: (1) baseline perf run with your traffic traces, (2) single‑model latency and throughput profiling across candidate gpu configs, (3) warm pool prewarm tests (simulate spikes), (4) KMS/key wrapping tests for encryption, (5) a small canary with real traffic routing, and (6) cost projection. we also do an SLO run to see 95/99 percentiles.

[00:08:18] Sofia: that sounds good. can you run the pilot on our on‑prem hardware? we have a small lab cluster with 4xA100 nodes for validation.

[00:08:25] Liam: yes we can deploy the private runtime in your lab cluster; we'll need cluster access and images. there are a few firewall/port requirements and you need to provide kernel modules for the accel libs. we'll share a preflight checklist.

[00:08:36] Evan: about the preflight checklist — include the KMS endpoints and what metadata Redwood needs for audit logs. also send any sample SAML/SSO config we need to fill.

[00:08:44] Maya: will do. Liam, can you confirm whether the pilot requires any paid commitment?

[00:08:49] Liam: most pilots are at no cost for a lightweight run, but if we need to reserve customer GPUs in our regional fleet for an extended controlled smoke test we sometimes ask for a small refundable fee. we'll call that out in the pilot plan.

[00:08:59] Rajiv: legal will ask about data residency for logs and model artifacts. we need the pilot plan to specify where data sits and how long it's retained.

[00:09:07] Maya: noted. we'll include data residency, retention, and AUP in the security packet.

[00:09:11] Sofia: one more thing — we use ephemeral container snapshots to map model versions. how do version pinning and rollbacks work?

[00:09:18] Liam: Redwood supports model version pinning per pool; rollbacks are a control plane operation with canary traffic ramp timeline. model artifacts can be stored in your artifact repo or Redwood's model store depending on private vs hosted. rollback is typically minutes if you have a prebuilt variant; full model load times depend on size and prewarm state.

[00:09:36] Rajiv: okay good. are there any typical gotchas for teams that move from self‑hosted k8s to Redwood Dedicated?

[00:09:42] Liam: common ones: (1) underestimating warmup times for very large shards, (2) token accounting differences across truncation strategies, (3) underestimate of prewarm node counts for unpredictable spikes, and (4) KMS routing complexity when mixing on‑prem keys with hosted burst. we document these and run a dry‑run.

[00:10:01] Maya: let's surface the follow‑ups: Liam will send pilot checklist + perf script; Maya will send draft pricing and SOW; Pandora team will share traffic traces and KMS details.

[00:10:12] Rajiv: yeah we'll aim to have that by monday.

[00:10:15] Evan: one quick security question — do you do attestation for on‑prem nodes or any FIPS validated libs?

[00:10:21] Liam: we support FIPS‑compatible crypto and can provide attestations for audited deployments; details in security packet. for on‑prem we'd work with your compliance team.

[00:10:30] Sofia: also, what's SLAs for dedicated reserved pools?

[00:10:33] Maya: reserved Dedicated has an SLA for availability and latency tiers depending on committed level. we'll include the SLA matrix in the packet.

[00:10:40] Rajiv: perfect. any other questions?

[00:10:43] Maya: client side, any SDK preferences? we have python/ts sdks, and grpc for low latency.

[00:10:49] Sofia: python SDK is what we use. grpc would be ideal for the low latency routes.

[00:10:53] Liam: we can wire up grpc, and we'll provide example clients.

[00:10:57] Rajiv: ok thanks, seems like a plan.

[00:11:00] Maya: recap of next steps and deadlines — Liam pilot checklist by 2025‑02‑18, Maya pricing/SOW by 2025‑02‑20, Pandora to share traces and KMS info by 2025‑02‑17.

[00:11:12] Rajiv: agreed. sound good to wrap.

[00:11:15] Evan: thanks everyone

[00:11:17] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links to the security docs and pilot plan. bye

[00:11:22] END TRANSCRIPT
